title: Testing Treatments and Tracing Causes
endLine: Randomize and blind to test treatments; track cohorts to trace causes.

scenes.tts: What if every patient taking a drug still gets worse? Could it still be working? Illness changes on its own, and knowing who got treated sways ratings. Clinical trials and epidemiology build fair comparisons instead.
scenes.caption: What if every patient taking a drug still gets worse? Could it still be working? Illness changes on its own, and knowing who got treated sways ratings. Clinical trials and epidemiology build fair comparisons instead.
scenes.visual: Open directly on the cohort stage filling most of the frame height: a crowd of softly drifting luminous dots moves left to right along a single sloping track that trends downward (schematic). A bold question appears at top: 'Getting worse — still working?' As the narrator speaks of illness changing and biased ratings, a hazy drift ripples through the track and a rater's clipboard tilts toward the curve; then the single track begins to split into two parallel lanes.
scenes.narration: What if every patient taking a drug still gets worse? Could it still be working? Illness changes on its own, and knowing who got treated sways ratings. Clinical trials and epidemiology build fair comparisons instead.

scenes.visual: The two-lane cohort stage dims slightly while the dots continue drifting gently; the title 'Testing Treatments and Tracing Causes' fades in large and clear, then fades out.

scenes.tts: To test a treatment fairly, split one group of people by chance. That chance split is a randomized trial, so both groups start alike. One group gets the treatment; the other gets a look-alike without the drug, a placebo. Neither patient nor rater knows which is which, keeping the trial double-blind.

scenes.visual: A mixed crowd of multi-shade dots enters a glowing chance gate (spinning coin-like shuffler) that routes dots unpredictably into the upper lane ('Treated', teal) and lower lane ('Placebo', warm gold), leaving both lanes with the same mix of shades. Identical plain pill icons (no molecular structures) appear on both lanes, one glowing inside and one empty. Opaque blinding covers slide over both lane labels and over the rater's clipboard at right, tagged 'Double-blind'.

scenes.tts: Take a large trial in early Alzheimer disease. People received lecanemab, an antibody that clears amyloid plaques, deposits between neurons, or a placebo for eighteen months. Suppose treated patients still got worse. What must the placebo group show if the drug helped?
scenes.caption: Take a large trial in early Alzheimer disease. People received lecanemab, an antibody that clears amyloid plaques, deposits between neurons, or a placebo for 18 months. Suppose treated patients still got worse. What must the placebo group show if the drug helped?
scenes.visual: On the same two-lane stage, the horizontal axis sets to '0 to 18 months' (tagged schematic). On the upper lane, labeled 'Lecanemab', dots travel rightward as a teal score curve slopes steadily downward; small faded plaque clusters along the lane shrink as dots pass (no molecular structures). The lower 'Placebo' lane stays hidden under an opaque mask with a large question mark. At top, the question fades in: 'What must the placebo curve do?'
scenes.narration: Take a large trial in early Alzheimer disease. People received lecanemab, an antibody that clears amyloid plaques, deposits between neurons, or a placebo for 18 months. Suppose treated patients still got worse. What must the placebo group show if the drug helped?

scenes.visual: The question remains clear at top while the downward teal 'Lecanemab' curve holds steady with drifting dots (schematic). Under the masked lower lane, three faint dashed gold curves pulse gently in turn — one above the teal curve, one overlapping it, and one dropping more steeply below it — giving viewers time to predict.

scenes.tts: The placebo group must decline faster. Both groups got worse, yet treated patients got worse more slowly. The gap between treated and placebo shows the effect: decline slowed without stopping. Random assignment and blinding separate a treatment's effect from bias, chance, and the disease's own course.
scenes.caption: The placebo group must decline faster. Both groups got worse, yet treated patients got worse more slowly. The gap between treated and placebo shows the effect: decline slowed without stopping. Random assignment and blinding separate a treatment's effect from bias, chance, and the disease's own course.
scenes.visual: The mask lifts off the lower lane: the gold 'Placebo' curve locks onto the steepest downward path below the teal 'Lecanemab' curve (schematic). Both curves slope down, and a bright vertical bracket lights up between them at 18 months with the simple comparison formula 'Effect = Treated − Placebo'. Subtle icons of the chance gate and blinding mask glow softly around the bracket as the guiding rule is spoken.

scenes.tts: Even a biological change can mislead without clinical outcomes. An autopsy deposit shows what builds up, not whether it kills. Trials judge clinical outcomes like thinking, daily function, or survival, and measure harms. In fragile X syndrome, mavoglurant in 2016 and basimglurant in 2018 were tested against placebo. Neither beat placebo on the main behavioural measures.

scenes.visual: On the right of the same stage, the outcome gauge shifts: a grey 'Biological deposit' dial dims and moves aside as a bright 'Clinical outcomes' panel expands showing three clean meters ('Thinking', 'Daily function', 'Survival') beside a 'Harms' dial (all schematic). Then the two lanes reset for fragile X syndrome ('Mavoglurant 2016', 'Basimglurant 2018'): the teal treated curve and gold placebo curve trace together, with overlapping shaded bands and no gap that stands out (schematic, no measured values).

scenes.tts: You cannot randomly assign a harmful drug or infection. Instead, epidemiology tracks groups of people, called cohorts, across time and place. A small cohort without an independent control shows feasibility, not population efficacy. Defects after isotretinoin exposure in 1985 fit animal results, yet the human mechanism stayed inferred.

scenes.visual: The chance gate dissolves as a soft stop bar crosses out random assignment of a hazard icon. The two lanes morph into a sweeping time-and-place map band where cohorts of glowing dots move through a shaded exposure wave (schematic). A tiny cluster of a few dots without a comparison band carries the short tag 'Feasibility only'. Then a 1985 timeline marker ('Isotretinoin 1985') links an exposed human cohort to an animal-result badge by a dashed line labeled 'Inferred' (schematic).

scenes.tts: Fair trials unlocked lasting prevention. A neural tube defect means the brain or spinal cord was left open. In 1991, the Medical Research Council Vitamin Study randomized women with a prior affected pregnancy. Four milligrams of folic acid daily, started before conception, cut recurrence by about seventy-two percent. That is about seven of every ten recurrences prevented.
scenes.caption: Fair trials unlocked lasting prevention. A neural tube defect means the brain or spinal cord was left open. In 1991, the Medical Research Council Vitamin Study randomized women with a prior affected pregnancy. 4 milligrams of folic acid daily, started before conception, cut recurrence by about 72 percent. That is about seven of every ten recurrences prevented.
scenes.visual: The stage returns smoothly to the two-lane randomized layout tagged 'MRC Vitamin Study, 1991'. Dots pass through the chance gate into 'Folic acid, 4 mg/day' (before conception) and 'Comparison'. On the right, two computed recurrence bars rise: the comparison bar sets the baseline, while the folic-acid bar drops by 72 percent below it (computed directly from the 72 percent reduction), with a crisp downward bracket marked '−72%'.

scenes.tts: In 1990, Delgado and colleagues studied twenty-one patients whose depression had remitted on antidepressants. Each patient received both a control and a challenge lowering tryptophan, serotonin's precursor, in double-blind crossover. Fourteen of the twenty-one relapsed after tryptophan depletion, while the control challenge had no significant effect.
scenes.caption: In 1990, Delgado and colleagues studied 21 patients whose depression had remitted on antidepressants. Each patient received both a control and a challenge lowering tryptophan, serotonin's precursor, in double-blind crossover. Fourteen of the 21 relapsed after tryptophan depletion, while the control challenge had no significant effect.
scenes.visual: The two lanes loop into a figure-eight crossover track tagged 'Delgado et al., 1990' with blinding covers over both halves. Exactly 21 luminous dots travel through both passes in swapped order (no molecular structures). On the 'Control' pass, the dots stay calm and steady. On the 'Tryptophan depletion' pass, fourteen of the 21 dots shift bright amber as a computed counter reads 'Fourteen of 21 relapsed'.

scenes.tts: Epidemiology then pairs with biology. In 2015 and 2016, microcephaly tracked Zika, matching a 2013 to 2014 French Polynesia outbreak. In 2016, Mlakar and colleagues found Zika virus particles in a fetal brain. Ming, Song, and Tang showed Zika kills some cultured human cortical progenitors and slows the rest. Fair trials test treatments; cohorts and biology together trace causes.

scenes.visual: The stage transforms back to the time-and-place cohort band (schematic): an epidemic wave rises across '2013–2014 French Polynesia' and '2015–2016', with a matching microcephaly wave tracking right behind it. Two clean evidence layers lock onto the wave: first a pathology lens showing tiny virus dots inside an outlined small fetal brain ('Mlakar et al., 2016', schematic), then a cell dish where dividing cortical progenitor cells slow and drop away ('Ming, Song & Tang, 2016', schematic). Finally, the randomized two-lane icon and the biology-linked cohort wave settle side by side in balance.
